analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal student aid to college programs that don't actually prepare students for required licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee in April 2015, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut off federal student aid — including Pell Grants, federal loans, and GI Bill benefits — to any college program claiming to prepare students for a licensed occupation unless graduates are actually qualified to get licensed in their own state, with required internships or clinical placements provided on time. It would also require the Education Department to write rules for not-yet-accredited programs and to make colleges sign loan-discharge agreements with students in those programs. Students at schools that currently sell degrees or certificates that don't meet state licensing requirements would gain the most.
analysis.who_benefits: Students in programs aimed at licensed jobs — nursing, allied health, trucking, cosmetology and similar fields — would be protected from paying tuition and taking on federal loans for credentials that don't qualify them to work in their state. Veterans using GI Bill benefits and other federal aid recipients would stop subsidizing these programs. Legitimate schools that already meet state licensing requirements would face a cleaner field against competitors selling unworkable credentials.

how_it_helps.text: A college program designed to prepare students for a licensed occupation would become ineligible for federal aid unless completing it actually qualifies students for the licensing exam and any certification required in their home state, and in any state the school advertises to.

Schools would have to provide timely placement in required pre-licensure steps like clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships, instead of leaving students to find them on their own after paying tuition.

The Education Department would have to write rules for programs that are not yet accredited — including limits on how they advertise — and make schools sign a loan discharge agreement with each student in such a program, giving students a path to have loans forgiven if the program doesn't deliver.

The protections would cover all major federal aid streams: Pell Grants and student loans under the Higher Education Act, workforce training funds under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, adult education funds, and veterans' and military education benefits under titles 38 and 10.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges whose licensed-occupation programs cannot meet the standard — chiefly for-profit career colleges — would lose access to federal student aid, which is their main revenue source, unless they restructure or shut the programs. The Education Department would bear the cost of writing the new regulations. Some compliant schools would face one-year compliance and documentation costs.

drawbacks.text: The one-year compliance deadline would be tight: schools would have to rework curricula, arrange clinical placements, and in some cases redesign programs across many states with different licensing rules, which could cause some schools to drop licensed-occupation programs rather than fix them.

Tying eligibility to qualification in the student's home state and in every state the school advertises to could burden schools that serve students across state lines, and the cost of compliance would likely be passed on to students in tuition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct: students would stop taking federal loans for credentials that don't let them get licensed to work. The main cost is compliance complexity for schools and a tight one-year runway, and the risk that some borderline programs close and reduce training slots. On balance the protections target a well-documented harm to student borrowers, and the compliance burden falls on the schools profiting from the problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles education in April 2015, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley, joined by Senator Dick Durbin, introduced the bill on April 30, 2015.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which is where the record ends.
The committee never held a hearing, voted on it, or reported it out, and no floor vote ever happened before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges — mainly for-profit career colleges — whose programs would have flunked the new standard kept their access to federal student aid for another two years, while students kept paying for credentials that may not meet licensing requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Substandard licensed-occupation programs kept federal aid

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the Senate cosponsor list shows one Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman during the 114th Congress, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split was recorded; both sponsors were Democrats and the bill sat untouched in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.note: These schools draw most of their revenue from federal student aid, and this bill would make any program that doesn't produce licensable graduates ineligible for that money. It would hit schools whose licensed-occupation programs — nursing, allied health, trades — leave graduates unable to sit for state licensing exams, and would also force loan-discharge deals on students in not-yet-accredited programs.

industries.industry: Community colleges and other accredited schools with licensed-occupation programs
industries.note: Most community college programs already map to state licensing requirements, so the direct cost is mainly one-year compliance and documentation work. Schools that do meet the standard would gain competitively as noncompliant rivals lose aid.
